Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I draw to the attention of this House an event of historical importance in Banff, Alberta, today. November 1, 1989, marks a significant step forward for the town in its advancement toward municipal government.
Starting today the mayor-elect, councillors, and school district trustees will join with the Banff Municipal Committee to facilitate the orderly transition of authority, for on January 1, 1990, through the co-operative effort of the Hon. Lucien Bouchard, the local authorities and the provincial government of Alberta, Banff will become a town with an elected mayor and council.

This $500 exemption can only be called a pittance in light of the costs incurred by these volunteers for such things as car insurance, clothing, cleaning bills and cost of gasoline, not to mention the danger that these men and women put
themselves in the path of. All of this is incurred in the name of community duty.
The minister has refused to raise the exemption to a well deserved $1,000. A few days ago the Auditor General advised that the Minister of Finance is "letting hundreds of millions of dollars slip through his hands". Further, the Auditor General, Mr. Dye, points out that nothing has been done to close the loopholes which represent a loss of revenue to the government in the order of $350 million a year.
I suggest that the minister's mistake is being compensated for at the expense of a fine group of people, a group of people that I think deserve our respect and, at this time, at least a little more in the exemption that they can claim. These are the very proud volunteer firemen of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, since the Auditor General's press conference, federal Liberals and New Democrats have constantly denounced the air travel expenses incurred by Members of our Government. Of course, they overlook the sound expenditure cuts made by our Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) to save Canadian taxpayers' money. For example, I would like to give the details of my latest trip in the North, where our Minister sent me to open the airports in Salluit and Kangirsujuaq from October 19 to 21. I went to Quebec City to take the Quebec Government's F-27. In two and a half days, I covered over 5,000 kilometres and my expenses were only $662.35 in all. This includes accommodation at the Confortel Motel in Quebec City for $47, lodging in Salluit and Montreal for $164, four meals for $32.35, two taxis for $15 and airfare of $404.
Mr. Speaker, this trip is the third of its kind that I have made at the Minister's request and we thus saved over $75,000. I congratulate the Minister and thank the Government of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, on September 28 the Secretary of State for External Affairs said that major banks co-ordinating South Africa's debt "agreed that they would be seeking the highest possible interest payments and the fastest possible repayments". As we all know, this did not materialize. In fact, South Africa won more favourable terms on its agreement with the banks for debt rescheduling. In light of the propaganda victory for South Africa, the words of our Secretary of State for External Affairs have become an embarrassment.
The strategy failure of this government with regard to South Africa demands that the Prime Minister immediately commit to his four-year-old promise made to the United Nations where he stated: "My government has said to Canadians that if there are not fundamental
changes in South Africa, we are prepared to invoke total sanctions against that country and its repressive regime".
Although we can hope the present government in South Africa may reconsider its apartheid policy, we know that it is increased sanctions, not hope, that will influence the required changes.
Lest the Prime Minister lose all credibility nationally and internationally with regard to his stated position to mount the necessary anti-apartheid policies, sanctions against South Africa must be increased today.

Mr. Speaker, on October 17, the FTA panel reported its conclusions on the B.C. salmon and herring issue. Canada is not bound to accept the ruling.
The decision to accept or not to accept would seem to pit the interests of fishermen against the interests of plant owners. One thing that is unclear is the implications of the panel decision for the Atlantic fishery, particularly in view of the Americans' apparent predisposition to apply the principles of the decision to the Atlantic fishery.
Seafood producers in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland fear that land-based processing jobs could be imperilled if the implication of the decision is that over-the-side sales could become rampant. On the other hand, fishermen could be short-term beneficiaries of higher prices.
Failure to accept the ruling would likely bring about immediate retaliation against east coast fisheries, particularly Nova Scotia lobsters.
I urge the government to use all the time available before making its decision. Possibly the best solution for all concerned would be to set the decision aside and to seek to negotiate an alternate agreement with the United States. In either case, full consultation should take place with all affected sectors and parties before any decision is taken or announced.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today under the provisions of Standing Order 31 to draw to the attention of the House that Polysar Limited of Sarnia, Ontario, was established by the Government of Canada during World War II. It has become a world class international petrochemical company operating in all global geographies.
It has provided employment opportunities to all production and corporate levels in the Sarnia-Lambton area over many years. This company has pioneered new technologies from its highly skilled research and development laboratories.
I bring to this House today my deep concern about rumours of impending layoffs in the Sarnia based operations of Polysar by Nova Corporation which acquired controlling interest in this company in 1988. This Sarnia operation is a world scale plant and has operated profitably over the years and, in several cases, employed technologies developed and introduced by Polysar.
There are early indications that the research activities are being curtailed. The consequences are serious for Canada in terms of our international competitiveness and the loss of opportunities for the graduates of our colleges and universities.
I call upon the government to investigate and report to the House on the impact of these cutbacks in the petrochemical industry and its research capabilities in this major and only Canadian owned petrochemical industry.
This government has a responsibility in this matter because it was through its policy of privatization that Polysar was purchased by another company, the priorities of which may not be research and development on a world scale. This company has been consistently profitable and it will be a major setback to Canada, and the Sarnia-Lambton region in particular, if these cutbacks take place.

speakeroldname: Hon. Doug Lewis (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
that Bill C-38, an act to amend the Federal Court Act, the Crown Liability Act, the Supreme Court Act and other acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to say at the outset how pleased I am to have the opportunity to bring forward this bill which contains amendments principally to the Federal Court Act and also to the Crown Liability Act. The over-all purpose of this legislation is to give the ordinary citizens who wish to sue the federal government
Government Orders
easier access to the Canadian courts and to reduce or eliminate the legal barriers and the inequities that a citizen now faces in such litigation.
First, I want to deal with the Federal Court Act proposals. It has been almost 20 years since the Federal Court was established. It was established to replace the old Exchequer Court and, although much of the jurisdiction that was conferred on this new court reflected the jurisdiction of the predecessor, there was also quite a bit that was new in this legislation. For example, the Exchequer Court at that time, as it was constituted, was only a trial level court and appeals from the decisions of the Exchequer Court were made directly to the Supreme Court of Canada. The act in 1971 established a new Federal Court of Appeal to hear the appeals from the decisions of the court's trial division.
Second, the Federal Court was granted an entirely new jurisdiction to supervise or review the activities and decisions of federal boards and tribunals. Generally I think it is fair to say that the establishment of the Federal Court a generation ago can be characterized as a bold and far-sighted experiment in reforming the federal civil justice system on behalf of all Canadians. It has proven itself to be invaluable to the Canadian system of justice, and it serves a number of special purposes that provincial courts cannot adequately fulfil.
First, the Federal Court is a Canada-wide court which has national jurisdiction. As a result it is not impeded by any territorial limitations on jurisdiction and on process to which the provincial courts are necessarily subject. The nation-wide quality of the Federal Court has proven essential for example in cases of admiralty and intellectual property, patents, copyright, trademarks and industrial design.
Second, the Federal Court is a court with specialized knowledge in a few specific areas. These include the Income Tax Act and other federal revenue laws, intellectual property and admiralty law.
The importance of the Federal Court to the Canadian legal system is evidenced by the fact that although the court and the provincial courts both have jurisdiction with respect to matters such as intellectual property and admiralty matters, most matters of this type are brought in the federal court.

November 1, 1989
Government Orders
Third, the Federal Court helps to ensure that the federal tribunals operate effectively, efficiently, and fairly throughout Canada under federal legislation that applies uniformly across the entire country.
I think it is appropriate at this time to pay tribute to the present Leader of the Opposition who as the Minister of Justice of the day in 1970 introduced legislation that established the court. Since that time there has been an opportunity for assessing the results of that experiment. I think it is fair to say that the Federal Court has proven to be an over-all success. But our assessment-and I think it is fair to say the assessment of the bar and others-has revealed a number of areas where improvements could be usefully made to the Federal Court Act and the related legislation.

Mr. Speaker, the major objectives of the proposals contained in this Bill are to facilitate access by individual Canadians to the federal civil justice system, to make that justice system fairer, to improve its efficiency and effectiveness and to improve service to the public provided by that system.
The first objective is that the Federal Court in particular and the federal justice system in general should be accessible to the ordinary citizen.
For example, a person should be able to sue the Crown in a suitably convenient court for breach of contract to purchase goods or for negligent driving by a Crown employee that causes injuries to another motorist. At the moment, such actions can only be brought in the Federal Court. However, it is not as available as provincial courts.
The Federal Court only has offices in the larger centres and judges of the Court, based as most of them are in the National Capital Region, are not as readily or as frequently available throughout Canada as are judges of provincial courts.
Moreover, for both citizen and lawyer alike, provincial courts, including their procedures and personnel, are much more familiar.
Therefore, the Federal Court is often not the most convenient one for the private litigant. With this in mind, the government has proposed that both the provincial courts and the Federal Court share jurisdiction with
respect to such actions, thereby generally giving the plaintiff a choice of forum.

Another example relates to the court supervisory jurisdiction. First of all that jurisdiction is now split in a confusing way between the trial division and the court of appeal.
Second, at the moment the Federal Court Act defines the court's general jurisdiction to supervise federal boards, commissions, and other tribunals solely by reference to the traditional common law remedies, many of which have Latin labels and are loaded with arcane technical baggage.
For example, among the remedies that are available in the trial division under the present provisions of section 18 are certiorari, mandamus, quo warranto and no one other than a person knowledgeable in administrative law or in Latin would probably have the remotest idea what sort of relief is offered by this language.
The bill deals with both these matters. The jurisdictional split between the two divisions of the courts will be removed, and everyday language is used to describe relief that the court can order, the grounds for obtaining that relief, and the procedure available to the individual for applying for that relief.
A second objective in the amendments is fairness. Fairness, with the powerful voice of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in support, strongly suggests that distinctions between litigants should be kept to a minimum and any that exist require a rational justification.
To illustrate this point, I would point to the present legislation which confers a number of special privileges and immunities on the Crown that no longer have quite the same justification as they once did. Of particular interest are the special notice requirements when the Crown is sued, and the immunity of the Crown from paying prejudgment interest. The bill will remove or modify these specific privileges and, in doing so, continue the trend of placing the Crown on a footing of greater equality with the ordinary citizen.
A third objective is to improve the efficiency and the effectiveness of the federal civil justice system. As I already mentioned, there is a confusing split in the supervisory jurisdiction of the trial division and the court of appeal. The bill clarifies exactly what remedies are
November 1, 1989

available, on what grounds, and where a citizen goes to obtain them, thereby reducing confusion, needless delay, duplication and expense.
A second area of inefficiency relates to the constitutional limitation on the federal court's jurisdiction in the field of Crown proceedings. The Crown can be sued but cannot sue in tort and contract in that court. The result has been that when an action is launched against the Crown in the Federal Court, the Crown must bring separate proceedings against the plaintiff or some other person in a provincial court. That is known as a counterclaim in third party proceedings. Remedies to eliminate this inefficient and wasteful method of disposing of Crown litigation is also addressed in the bill.
The fourth objective is to improve more generally service to the public by the federal civil justice system. In support of the objective to improve access to the public, the government proposes in this bill to transfer to provincial courts full responsibility for compensation appeals under a number of agriculture statutes. In addition a number of provisions, which provide for an absolute bar to a suit against the Crown if certain notice requirements are not fulfilled, will be repealed.
Moreover, the review of decisions and activities of federal administrative bodies will be conferred on the trial division rather than the Court of Appeal. Since matters at the trial division are reviewed by a single judge as compared to the three judges when an appeal is heard, litigants will have more flexibility and improved access to the court.
This proposal will also enable members of the Appeal Court to devote more of their time to considering cases of broad public importance.

Proceeding to the bill itself, Mr. Speaker, and before giving detailed consideration to its provisions, I believe it may be useful to list, briefly and generally, the reforms the Bill contains.
First of all, whereas at present ordinary common law and civil law actions for relief against the federal Crown can only be brought in the Federal Court, as mentioned
Government Orders
earlier, under the bill that jurisdiction will be shared with provincial courts.
Second, an entirely new regime for supervising the validity and legality of the activities of the federal government is being established.
Third, the provisions of the Federal Court Act that govern appeals from the Federal Court to the Supreme Court of Canada are being transferred to the Supreme Court Act.
In that way, appeals from provincial courts and the Federal Court to the Supreme Court of Canada will all be dealt with together in the same statute.
Fourth, drawing on the experiences of some of the provinces, a representative rules committee composed of Federal Court judges and representatives of the legal profession and the Attorney General is being established to make the rules of the court.
This Committee will include judges of the Federal Court, representatives of the legal profession and the Attorney General, who will work together to improve court proceedings.

Fifth, modifications to some of the procedural advantages now enjoyed by the Crown are being made. These include the repeal of some of the special notice requirements in the Crown Liability Act and the imposition of responsibility on the Crown to pay prejudgment interest.
Sixth, consequent upon the increased role of provincial courts in the area of Crown proceedings, it is necessary that there be legislation dealing generally with practice and procedure when the Crown is a party to litigation. At present such matters are duplicated by the Federal Court Act and the Crown Liability Act simply because the latter is restricted in scope to actions against the Crown in tort, that is, civil wrongs of a non-contractual nature. All such provisions are being consolidated and are retitled Crown Liability and Proceedings Act. The Federal Court Act itself will no longer provide specifically, as it does now, for such matters.
Seventh, a few minor changes to the admiralty provisions of the Federal Court Act are being made. The definition of "ship" is being updated to bring it in conformity with recent changes to the meaning of that word in the Canada Shipping Act.

Government Orders
As well, authority is being conferred on the Federal Court to improve the scope of remedies available to the owner of the ship which has suffered damage.
That, in a nutshell, is what the bill proposes to do. In summary, this proposed legislation is going to improve access by Canadians to the courts. It is going introduce greater fairness into the federal civil justice system and will enhance the efficiency and the effectiveness of that system.
We think that this measure is a step forward and will provide Canadians with a more rational, comprehensible and open process for litigating matters with the federal government.

Consequently, I urge Members of this House to give this Bill their full support.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity today to speak to this badly needed and long awaited reform to the Federal Court Act, the Crown Liability Act, the Supreme Court Act and several other federal statutes, generally all pertaining to the federal court procedures and technical requirements which our members of the public must follow or endure as they involves themselves in litigation or contest with the federal government or federal interests.
One of the outstanding issues surrounding this particular set of reforms is the length of time that it has taken to reach this stage. I practised law for approximately 15 years prior to being elected to this House.
I want to set out at this time my view that the delay of many years, about 10 years, in putting these reforms in place has cost all of us as taxpayer who pay for the government and individual litigants millions of dollars in terms of costs, being the costs of the inefficiency and duplication that were found in the federal court system and procedures.
For example, an individual litigant who found himself or herself on the losing end of an administrative decision would be forced to take a decision as to whether or not an appeal was appropriate. Even if that person had the finest of cases and could see the error in judgment of the tribunal of first instance, that person was usually faced with a trip to the downtown of one of our major cities and a potential retainer of $2,000 to $5,000. That is a
huge hurdle in attempting to achieve the justice that our litigation system and our federal tribunals initially set out to achieve.
The reforms that have been proposed now are just not for lawyers, but they are for the public as well. They remove ambiguity, they broaden jurisdiction appropriately, they remove some technical limitations, and they streamline procedures. I know those are probably the words of the hon. minister and the government, but as a practising solicitor prior to arriving here I concur that these technical changes are long overdue and they will produce real savings and efficiencies in the cost of litigation.
Up to now it has been common to commence litigation by issuing a filing process in both the Federal Court and the superior court of the province. Not only was it a wasteful duplication, but it also required the lawyer and the support staff to devote resources to the avoidance of technical or other obstacles in both courts. There is a veritable mine field of obstacles out there from the legal point of view. That this relatively non-controversial set of reforms remained unrectified for so long is I think a bit of an embarrassment to this Parliament.
The purpose of our court system is to provide a means of dispute resolution for our society, generally between persons and organizations, persons and government, and to provide a system of disclosure and balance of interest within a democratically constituted legal framework.
But other barriers remain in our justice system now, and the average person out there is very aware of it. The initiative for reform was on the table at least five or six years ago. The list of housekeeping chores that had to be accomplished, which was brought forward by the legal profession, by people in government and by judges, was on the table. We were all well aware of them. There are still inefficiencies and other outstanding business in the field of justice that we must look at.
One of the areas that we should be aware of is the cut-backs recently to the federal government program to support litigation on public issues. These cut-backs affect litigation that pertains to what I would call the leading edge of development of legal principles in our society. That leading edge is very important in securing a balance of interest between the people of the country and the government. To the extent that these cut-backs
November 1, 1989

retard the development of this leading edge of litigation, all of our society will pay the price for the delay.
Another matter we should recall is one that I have raised in this House previously. It is my sense that the government for many reasons has acquiesced in a nondisclosure on the part of institutions or publicly elected officials in areas where the public has I think rightfully asked questions about the appropriateness of conduct, the appropriateness of spending of tax dollars. I think of plea bargaining which in some courts will prevent the public from knowing the factual basis for charges. That is in the criminal court. In the civil court there is bargaining in settlement of litigation which will prevent disclosure of the real issues lying behind the litigation.
We heard today a suggestion that because a public official sits in the other place there is some general immunity from the laws of this land, that perhaps those laws do not apply through our government quite the same way as they apply to members in this House. From the point of view of the citizen and the taxpayer I have to ask the question: Where is the balancing of interest? Where are the mechanisms to achieve that balance of interest?
Procedural obstacles and conflicts between our immigration laws and our extradition laws are again another problem. I know the Minister of Justice recently carried out his administrative or quasi-judicial function in dealing with the matter under the Extradition Act involving an individual by the name of Charles Ng. Almost every day there is an article in the paper about some alleged killer from another country who is here illegally. He is staying in custody at our expense. He does not want to go back to his or her country to face the music. I ask: Where is the justice there? I think I read yesterday that we had one of these individuals actually attending school, taking a course, I guess at our expense.
The conflict here is that our Extradition Act and our Immigration Act have been developed separately in terms of procedures. As a result, the citizen of this country, the taxpayer, is unable to pursue directly the course of justice that should be there. It is perhaps unfortunate that the burden of that lies upon a minister
Government Orders
of the government as opposed to a tribunal or a procedure already existing in government. That is an area that also requires attention from the justice point of view.
Another matter involves the decision of the Supreme Court in The Queen versus Morgentaler. In that action an entire provision of the Criminal Code has been removed. If there was justice for the unborn, for the life that lives in the womb in the days or weeks prior to birth, where is it now with that provision removed?
It has been approximately two years since it became clear to most of us in the country that the Young Offenders Act was failing to adequately serve some interests of society. I think it is inappropriate for this government to permit us to continue with a statute that treats a killer like a child. I think most of us would agree with that without too much argument. I know this Parliament will have an opportunity to look at reforms, but those reforms are long in coming and we must address them quickly.
My hope from this side of the House is that the government will acknowledge that matters of justice are just as important as other matters of government. They are just as important to the citizens of this country as old age security, environment, trade, taxation and other matters we deal with in our federal government. I hope that with the government's magnificent success in achieving these existing reforms in this Bill C-38, achieved after 10 years of thinking and paper pushing, this success will spur this government to improve its record in the field of justice.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to participate in this debate on the proposed amendments to the provisions of the various acts, both the Federal Court Act and the Crown Liability Act dealing with the Federal Court.
I listened with care to the comments of both the minister and my colleague from Scarborough-Rouge River. I am not going to canvass the waterfront of justice issues in the very limited time I will be taking to respond on behalf of the New Democratic Party on this important legislation. I did note, however, that the hon. member made some reference to the provisions of the Criminal

Government Orders
Code on abortion and suggested we should recriminalize this area of the law.
I must ask: Who is it that speaks on behalf of the Liberal party on this very important and difficult issue of abortion? Is it the hon. member for Scarborough- Rouge River? Is it the leadership candidate from Scarborough West? Is it the leader of the Liberal party? Is it the member for Halifax, the spokesperson on the status of women who says we do not need a new criminal law? Who is it today that speaks for the Liberal party on this very important and sensitive question?
We have heard the call from the member for Scarborough-Rouge River for new criminal law in this area. I say on behalf of the New Democrats that we believe that there is no need whatsoever for recriminalization of this area of the law. Indeed, changes to the Canada Health Act are necessary to ensure equitable access. It is an insult to the women of this country and to doctors in this country to suggest that we have to go back to those dark days of criminal sanctions in this area.

speechtext: On a point of order, the hon. member for Leeds-Grenville.

Mr. Speaker, if this is supposed to be a debate on abortion I think we should have had some notification that we are having a debate on abortion this afternoon. I am critically interested in the topic. I think we should get back to the bill at hand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: On debate, the member for Burnaby-Kingsway.

Mr. Speaker, I was merely picking up the theme that was introduced by the hon. member's own colleague during the debate. I would welcome the views of yet another Liberal member on this question. I am sure we will have yet another variety.
The hon. member also spoke on the question of the Young Offenders Act. We all recognize the deep concerns that exist about the quality of the delivery of justice in the area of young offenders. I would, however, remind the hon. member who was so critical of the Young Offenders Act that that piece of legislation was introduced by his own colleague, the member for York
Centre. He may want to have a word with his colleague about the provisions of that legislation.
TUrning to the provisions of the Federal Court Act and the Crown Liability Act, I note that Bill C-38 is legislation which represents the first major change to the Federal Court Act and the Crown Liability Act since the Federal Court Act was introduced in 1971. For those Canadians who are not familiar with the Federal Court, perhaps it is appropriate to comment briefly on the jurisdiction of that body.
The Federal Court, which includes both the Trial Division and the Federal Court of Appeal, was established by Parliament in 1971 to deal with, among other things, lawsuits against the federal government, cases based wholly on federal law, patents and copyright for example, maritime law, interpretation of the Access to Information Act, the Privacy Act, and challenges to decisions by federal tribunals, the Tariff Board and the Pensions Appeal Board, for instance.
In the area of access to information and privacy, I might just note that the current conservative government has displayed utter contempt for the parliamentary process in rejecting the unanimous recommendation of the Standing Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General to strengthen the provisions of the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act. Promises were made by the late Walter Baker to strengthen this legislation which, after all, is at the heart of our democratic system, the right of citizens to have free and open access to the information which forms the basis for government decision-making. This government has failed miserably in making information available to Canadian citizens.
There have been a number of concerns arising about the jurisdiction of the Federal Court. It is an incredibly complicated area of law. A lawsuit, for example, which involves claims against both the federal government and private individuals, corporations or other governments can be very, very complicated. In some cases, such a lawsuit cannot be disposed of in one court alone. It actually has to be taken in a number of different courts.
One example of this was the litigation that arose from the 1978 crash at the Cranbrook airport. In that instance, the plaintiff airline brought action against the federal Ministry of Transport, various Crown servants, the city of Cranbrook, various city employees and the manufacturers of the airplane and the plane's thrust reversers. The

Trial Division of the Federal Court decided that while the Ministry of Transport had to be sued in Federal Court, ministry employees, like other defendants, had to be sued separately in the B.C. Supreme Court since their liability was governed by common law.
There are many other examples of a similar nature of the confusion in jurisdiction between the Federal Court and provincial superior courts.
As well, the second major area of difficulty was with respect to the division of responsibility between the Trial Division of the Federal Court and the Federal Court of Appeal in challenges to the decisions of tribunals. That has been an area that has caused difficulty and confusion for some time. Indeed, lawyers would frequently file documents in both the Federal Court Trial Division and the Federal Court of Appeal just so they would not make a mistake or miss out on a limitation period. Obviously that kind of situation is one that is not only unfair to the legal profession but ultimately is unfair to Canadian litigants generally who have a right to clarity in the law. I want to say, on behalf of the New Democrats, that we certainly welcome the general thrust of the amendments that have been brought forward by the minister in this area.
I want to raise an issue of concern with respect to process. The minister received on October 6 last, a little less than a month ago, a letter from the Attorney General of the Province of British Columbia, Bud Smith. In that letter, the Attorney General of British Columbia indicates that following consultations with provincial and territorial Attorneys General they were unanimous in their view that the issue of the continuation of the Federal Court of Canada as presently constituted was a matter which they all felt merits further consideration and study.
We all know the position of the Attorney General of British Columbia. It has been his position for some time. I have a paper here that was prepared by Bud Smith in which he states that the long-standing position of British Columbia with respect to the Federal Court of Canada has been that the establishment of the Federal Court of Canada is wholly unnecessary and is not only a wasteful expenditure of public funds but has resulted and will yet
Government Orders
result in practical disadvantages and inconveniences to the citizens of Canada.
That is the position of the Attorney General of British Columbia. I do not think it is fair to suggest that that is a position shared by the colleagues of the Attorney General of British Columbia from other provinces or the territories. I certainly would not suggest for a minute that that is the case. What is clear is that all Attorneys General at the recent meeting in June of this year in Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, directed their deputies to study this possibility. That study is under way. At the same time, as I understand it, the Federal Law Reform Commission is looking at the whole question of the role of the Federal Court and the jurisdiction of it.
The Canadian Bar Association decided just a month ago to reactivate its committee of the 1970s on the matter of the Federal Court and to prepare a report by December of this year in order that the council of the Canadian Bar Association might take a position at its mid-winter meeting in February, 1990.
Speaking on behalf of the Attorneys General, Bud Smith urged the Minister of Justice to postpone the introduction of this bill, or at the very least, to postpone debate at second reading, until the Canadian Bar Association report had been considered by the council of the CBA and until the Law Reform Commission had made its views known on this important question as well. I regret that the Minister of Justice has refused to heed this call not only from the attorney general of British Columbia but from attorneys general of at least eight other provinces and territories as well.
This is an issue which obviously has to be moved on, but it has now been many years since the original proposals were made. I think it has been over 10 years since the Canadian Bar Association's study in this area. I would have thought the minister might have waited just a few more months before proceeding in the rather highhanded way that he has proceeded.
The government has claimed to be concerned about consultation with the provinces. Here is an illustration where provincial governments, through the attorneys general, have asked for consultation and have asked for delay. The federal Minister of Justice says, "No, I am going to proceed without agreement".

November 1, 1989
Government Orders
So I wanted, both as a member of Parliament from British Columbia and as the spokesperson on justice for the New Democratic Party, to raise that concern about process and to urge the minister to consider the possibility of delaying any further proceedings on this legislation until such time as both the Canadian Bar Association and the Law Reform Commission have been given an opportunity to make their views known.
At the very least I am pleased to have received an earlier assurance from the minister that in committee proceedings there will be full opportunity for representatives of the Attorneys General, the Canadian Bar Association, the Law Reform Commission and others to voice their concerns at an appropriate time. I would hope that perhaps there might be some delay in this area.
Naturally, a number of the proposed changes flow from recommendations of the Canadian Bar Association from 1977 and from the report of the Law Reform Commission issued three years later.
I referred earlier to the two main areas of confusion about the Federal Court, the distribution of jurisdiction between the Federal Court and the existing provincial superior courts and the division of responsibility between the Trial Division and the Federal Court of Appeal. I am not going to summarize the jurisdiction of the Federal Court at this time. That has been done by the minister in his comments. To the extent that Bill C-38 attempts to resolve some of the confusion, uncertainty and difficulty that has arisen with respect to jurisdiction, those are changes that we in general terms support.
We welcome as well the changes in the bill that would abrogate certain long-standing advantages enjoyed by the Crown such as not having to pay interest on damages for the period before judgment. That was always unfair. I am pleased the minister has brought forward changes that will ensure the Crown does, in fact, pay interest on damages before judgment as well as post-judgment.
I am not going to go through some of the key areas that are covered by the bill because, once again, that has been touched on. There is a requirement now that parties before the Federal Court give notice to the Attorney General of Canada and the Attorney General of each province when a constitutional question is to be
argued. In general terms, once again, that is not something with which we would have any difficulty.
There is a provision in the bill that removes a requirement that litigants give the Deputy Attorney General of Canada advance notice of a legal claim against the Crown. There is a new remedy that will allow the courts to issue an order declaratory of the rights of parties in certain proceedings. While injunctions and specific performance are not to be granted against the Crown, at least there is the opportunity for declaratory relief, and that is a step forward.
The amendments, as I say, in general terms are amendments which we welcome. The removal of the dilemma in having to choose between the Trial Division and the Court of Appeal is welcome. I know that the hon. member for Halifax, a distinguished legal counsel with extensive experience in the Federal Court, will be sharing that with us at an appropriate time. I am sure she would agree that her experience in the Federal Court would lead her as well to support these amendments which have given rise to such confusion and such uncertainty.
I want to raise a couple of other areas of concern, while I am on my feet, with respect to access to justice. That is part of what this whole process is about. We know, of course, that in the area of judicial appointments unfortunately the history of the Federal Court is not a happy one. In fact, in the report of the Canadian Bar Association on the appointment of judges in Canada, it was noted that political favouritism has been a dominant, though not sole, consideration in appointments to the Federal Court of Canada.
Too frequently the Federal Court has been a repository for friends of the government. I am speaking of both the Liberal government, which engaged in that orgy of excessive patronage in June of 1984 including appointments to the Federal Court, as well as the current government. Let us hope that this history of patronage appointments to the Federal Court will soon be a thing of the past.
We are watching with interest the new appointments process.

And I must say that I am very happy to see the role played by several conservative members from Quebec that have long been looking for ways to improve the
November 1, 1989

system whereby judges are appointed. Mr. Speaker, the new system should hopefully curtail patronage appointees, both conservative and liberal. Time will tell! There are always problems in this regard, but we want to see the best men and women appointed to courts of all levels in Canada.

I mention as well the importance of appointing women. While certainly it is true that this government and this minister has appointed a number of women to the bench, there is still significant work to be done in that area. Given the history of the previous conservative governments, I would note that prior to 1984, no conservative government had ever appointed a single woman to the federal judiciary. That is slowly changing and I certainly welcome the recent improvement in the number of women who have been appointed, but further work remains to be done in that area.
Certainly recent commissions of inquiry in the area of access to the law by native people have demonstrated glaring problems in this area, including the Marshall inquiry in Nova Scotia, the inquiry into the delivery of justice to native people in Manitoba and the inquiries in Alberta, British Columbia and elsewhere. Our treatment of native people in the law has been shameful and I would appeal to the minister to examine far more seriously than he has done the proposal for a justice system which would be a parallel justice system for native people. It has been a recommendation of the Canadian Bar Association and it is one that the minister should not reject out of hand as he has done.
We want as well to ensure that our bench more accurately reflects the multicultural nature of this country. Again, there has been small progress but not nearly enough, there is deep concern about the level of the government's commitment in this area. This is a government which is still not prepared to allow our national police force, the RCMP, to reflect that multicultural heritage, a government which has a minister who refuses to accept the recommendation of the commissioner of the RCMP to make this very reasonable change in the uniform, a government which is still listening to the Neanderthal voices of certain members of the Alberta caucus on this question, stirring up an atmosphere that unfortunately has led to badges with symbols of banning turbans. That has got to change and an important part of
Government Orders
reflecting the multicultural reality of our country is to ensure that it is reflected on the bench as well.
Speaking as well of such a fundamental question as access to the courts, I must underline my concern and the concern of my colleagues at both the provincial and federal levels about the serious under-funding of legal aid programs, a terribly difficult problem. Those who want access to the courts, not just federal courts but to courts at all levels, are too frequently denied that access particularly in the area of civil litigation, because they cannot afford to go to the courts. I would appeal to the government and to the Minister of Justice to show leadership in this area and to ensure that legal aid programs receive significant increases in funding.
Another area in which the federal government must show leadership with respect to access to the courts is in renewal of the funding of the Federal Court challenges program. The minister spoke of the charter and some of the new challenges facing the judiciary under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Litigants who cannot afford to bring their cases before the courts are obviously denied that element of justice. As Frank Scott said, the trappings of democracy hang loosely on an emaciated body politic. It is so true, and if the court challenges fund is not renewed, then those individuals who want to have access to the courts to pursue charter challenges will be denied that access.
I want to emphasize again that certainly in principle we support this legislation, and the changes that have been proposed in many instances are long overdue. The bill will introduce an element of equity and fairness into a system which is too often confusing and unfair. It is legislation that will require careful study in the legislative committee which has been appointed to consider it.
I would hope as well that there might be an opportunity for us to call some of the witnesses I mention, the representatives of the attorneys general, the law Reform Commission, the Canadian Bar Association and others. There is still much work to be done in this area; the gain in terms of general concerns in the judiciary area, the whole concept of citizenship court judges. We know that the Canadian Judicial Council in its recently issued first report has recommended changes in this area. No longer will these people be considered as judges but rather they ought to be considered for what they are a type of commissioner. Obviously this is another area which has

November 1, 1989
Government Orders
been rife with patronage but it is one in which we hope there will be changes.
The law of contempt of court is an issue that must be addressed as well. Again, we have to ask ourselves whether we should not consider the recommendations of a number of distinguished Canadians, including a former justice of the Supreme Court of Canada, Justice Willard Estey, who suggested that there should be a role for Parliament in the appointment process of federally appointed judges. As he points out:
- the closed circuit system we use in Canada doesn't allow much
input by the democratic basement of our community, the electorate.
It's all based upon the theory that you elect good people who in turn
appoint good people. That's a debatable formula.
Fortunately, we have in general terms been well served by our judiciary in this country but much work remains to be done, work with respect to access to the courts and to the justice system for Canada's first nations, for native people, ensuring that women are appointed to the judiciary and ensuring that judges are sensitized to the concerns of sexual equality in this country. Too frequently we see examples of an absence of awareness of the importance of equality in sexual assault trials. For example, comments are made which are not only offensive and sexist but completely unacceptable in this country.
In closing, I once again want to emphasize that we do support in principle Bill C-38 which is before the House. We will be urging in committee a number of improvements to the bill and particularly urging that those witnesses from the Law Reform Commission, the Canadian Bar Association and the Attorneys General be given an opportunity to appear before the committee. Let us hope that these changes will ensure more justice in the judicial system in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today with some concerns regarding this bill, but in general, I can say it certainly is an idea whose time has come. In actual fact, its time had come a number of years ago.
I also want to commend my honourable colleague from Burnaby-Kingsway for his very kind mention of me and my experience in the Federal Court, but I must give over to him because I do understand that his
experience in the Federal Court is far more extensive than my own and I understand that it may possibly be even more extensive than that of the Hon. Minister of Justice across the way.
However, I do want to make a few points in particular with regard to the topic that we are addressing today, namely, amendments to the Federal Court Act. It may not be the most riveting and the most exciting legislation for members of this House. It may not make it to the national news, the local news or indeed any news. But it is terribly important in the over-all legal scenario that we as legislators and as lawyers attempt to create in this country.
There are many problems with the legal system in this country, but I believe the major problem is the mystification of the process. Those of us who are legally trained, who practise law and have now turned to a second avocation of the lawyer, that of a legislator, realize from our past experience the fear and trepidation with which many Canadians go to law. It is a system that seems burdened with its own language, its own shibboleths and its own difficult and tortuous paths which are completely unintelligible to the vast majority of everyday people. Consequently, anything that helps to demystify the process is to be appreciated and perhaps from time to time even applauded.
For lawyers, the proposed amendments will surely be welcome. Changes in the Federal Court Act pertaining to judicial review will eliminate the dilemma in choosing between the Trial Division or the Court of Appeal. Experienced lawyers are, at the present time, filing two requests, one before each court, in order to get around the limitation period and to be sure that at least one request will be fully heard and not rejected on a preliminary motion.
In cases against the Crown, these changes will make it much easier for lawyers to take the proceedings before the superior court in their own provinces where they generally have more expertise. Ultimately this will benefit people who sue the Crown.
The problem again is the one of burgeoning legal class in this country, the inability of our government or indeed our system to provide a judicare system anywhere close to our medicare system for reasons that are obvious to

anyone who has ever had to go through the trauma and the costly experience of going to court.
There are several questions with regard to these amendments that I would like to bring forward today. Bill C-38 and its amendments to the Federal Court Act follows recommendations long put forward by both the Canadian Bar Association and the Law Reform Commission. As a matter of fact, some of these recommendations go back as far as 1977.1 have here The Federal Court Act, a Study of the Court's Administrative Law Jurisdictions, which is of interest to me and to others for a variety of reasons. One reason is that it was written by a well-known legal scholar in this country, David Mullen, a former professor of mine. Even more so, and I would draw this to the attention of all members of the House, footnote No. 187 in this brilliant work of legal scholarship mentions my hon. colleague, the member for Ottawa South, who unfortunately is not here today. The erudition and the ability as a legal scholar cited by my hon. colleague is one that would be of benefit to all members to take under advisement.
With regard to the bill itelf and the amendments, in 1983 the Law Reform Commission issued a report which ostensibly recommended the amendments that are being brought forward today. I know that all of us are experienced with, in the Shakespearean phrase, the law's delays, but six years is a little excessive. I think that the people of Canada might want to know what took so long in getting these amendments, laudable as they are, finally to the floor of the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Trying to get up the excitement level?

Chill out, Mr. Minister, it gets more exciting as we go on. I have more questions for you, none of which you are prepared to answer but I will certainly give it a try. Unfortunately, I may not be at the committee, Mr. Minister, and I have you here as a semi-captive audience and I will attempt at least to plant the seeds of these questions in his mind where I am sure they will find fallow ground.
There's no problem, he's open-minded.
Do you think? Those people from New Brunswick are so idealistic.

Seeds don't sprout in the dark.
Government Orders
Now, now, heckle him, don't heckle me. You're on my side.
Oh, oh!

At any rate, in 1983, the report of the Department of Justice allegedly has been put to a study and has been reconsidered. If this is so, I wonder why the Minister of Justice has not at some point revealed the results of such a departmental study or the examination thereto to the public at large. I should not suppose, given the subject matter that it probably is anything of great embarrassment to the government, but it might perhaps increase the demystification of what is ostensibly a fairly mystifying process to people in general.
Some of the changes in Bill C-38 grant to the Federal Court jurisdiction concurrent with that of provincial superior courts. I am wondering if there was consultation with provincial counterparts of the Minister of Justice in order to obtain their opinions on these changes as some of the provincial courts are already overburdened. I perhaps could be suggesting that the Minister of Justice get on with it and appoint more judges in certain provinces. Certainly some of the appointments he has made I have already congratulated him on privately and I will now do so here publicly. Some changes, note that, some. Can the Minister of Justice explain when the significant part of the Federal Court's jurisdiction is concurrent with that of these provincial superior courts why he did not take advantage in the reforms in Bill C-38 to reduce the concurrent powers of the Federal Court? Would not this reduction of the Federal Court's jurisdiction have allowed the federal government to reduce expenditures required for the administration of the court and do what it wants to do so badly in every other area of Canadian life, reduce the deficit?
Perhaps if it had reduced some of this concurrent jurisdiction and the expenditures thereto we would not be sitting here mourning-certainly the way they are mourning in my region of Atlantic Canada-by the cutting off and the strangling of the unemployment insurance program. I merely say that as a suggestion to the hon. minister because I know that underneath that cruel exterior there is a soft heart.

I would sure like to see it.

November 1, 1989
Government Orders

Aha! Now we have heckling from the minister's side. There is a light at the end of this tunnel.
The provincial superior courts as well have long experience in matters involving suits against a provincial Crown. I wonder again why the provincial superior courts could not have been given exclusive jurisdiction as well over actions against the federal Crown.
The Law Reform Commission and the Canadian Bar Association have been lobbying for a time, and indeed I have mentioned this to the minister, to have some of the peripheral criminal matters that are currently in the Federal Court's jurisdiction with regard to certain federal statutes transferred. From my own experience as a provincial and municipal prosecutor in the past, I recall that there are criminal sanctions, not just attached to the Income Tax Act but to various acts such as the Small Birds Act, the Customs and Excise Act and a number of other federal statutes.
These are recommendations of both the Canadian Bar Association and the Law Reform Commission to ensure that the Federal Court is not, with the greatest of respect to that court, getting involved in criminal matters which in the opinion of both of these august bodies are better off in the other court system.
Prior to considering any amendments to the judicial review of administrative tribunals, can the Minister of Justice tell us if he has reviewed the provisions of the provincial statutes in this regard? Can he also explain why he did not refer more to the pertinent provisions in provincial statutes which are simpler and more comprehensive?
Again, it is a question of demystification of the legal process. The people of Canada are basically suspicious of and live in a certain amount of fear and trepidation with regard to the legal process. I do believe that it is our duty as legislators to in every way make this process more comprehensible to the people of this country. I am sure that the minister does agree with me and that these oversights will be corrected at the earliest possible date. But then again, I always was an optimist.
With regard to the amendments in general, I can say that they are long awaited, and while we do not feel that they go far enough, they do make in the long run an honest effort to begin a process long needed, not just in
the Federal Court Act and the other statutes pertaining thereto but in the legal system generally.
In closing, I would like to refer to a quote from political scientist Peter Russell. In his recent book, The Judiciary in Canada he said:
Rather than simply adding judges to the (Courts) to cope with this expansion in administrative law cases, the government should pursue the proposals set out in the 1983 MacGuigan paper and reduce the court's role in fields where it has no special expertise and which overlap with the jurisdiction of the provincial superior courts. In this way, the benefits of developing a court with a special competence in some complex area of federal law (like the judicial review of federal authorities) can be realized while curtailing the drift toward a dual court system.
I think that these sentiments add to those sentiments expressed here today of the need to make the legal system in this country more relevant to the people and more comprehensible to the people. In this particular area the government has made one small step. Perhaps, in the words of Neil Armstrong, it should look toward making one giant step.
