speakerposition: subtopic
stagedirection
speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, October 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-29, an Act to establish the Department of Forestry, to amend the Forestry Development and Research Act and to make related amendments to other Acts, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, although we have the assurance that this Bill will be passed unanimously on third reading, I would still


November 1, 1989

like to submit a few comments to the House, to highlight the amendments passed in the legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-29, an act to establish the department of forestry. I feel that this particular bill has been rushed through its stages, but by no means should it be interpreted as a non-controversial or unimportant piece of legislation.
The creation of a forestry department is a step in the right direction. After hearing time and time again the same complaints from witnesses before the legislative committee, the press and the opposition, I do believe that the government is starting to get the message.
I must reiterate, as I have done in previous speeches time and again, that the forestry industry provides one in ten jobs in Canada directly or indirectly. In fact, close to
800,000	people work in the industry and 350 communities depend on it.
I am very pleased to say that there was a certain amount of flexibility that took place in the legislative committee. There were a total of five amendments passed. This shows that the government realized that the bill could be improved and it has put forth certain efforts to try to correct certain aspects of this bill.
To the preamble my colleague from Restigouche- Chaleur introduced an amendment which was accepted unanimously. The definition of sustainable development proposed by my colleague echoes the one devised by Dr. Gro Harlem Brundtland, the former Norwegian Prime Minister and Chairman of the United Nations World Commission on Environment and Development. "The defining of sustainable development in law, as a development which meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, is a very significant step", the hon. member for Restigouche-Chaleur said. Many environmental groups have criticized the federal government for using a term which lacks a standard definition and which may be easily misconstrued.
"This definition ensures that the forestry department will play a key role in the preservation of Canada's valuable woodlands. Moreover, it clearly establishes a
Government Orders
term that the government has been recklessly brandishing about", the hon. member further stated.

On a more personal note, I also wish the minister would do what he suggested last July, when he said:
We should send an offer to the Americans, to sound them out
before sending them a termination notice.
To my amazement, nothing has been done so far. That is really too bad!

On October 27, in the House, the minister's answer to my question was very disappointing. At one point he stated that the 15 per cent surtax on softwood lumber was a minor factor. I found that incredible. He categorically stated in July that the 15 per cent surtax has had an effect on the Canadian softwood lumber industry. If it is so minor, why is he planning to send a termination notice? On the other hand, I was pleased to hear him say that he is constructing the evidence that would provide him with the necessary authority and jurisdiction to renegotiate the MOU. I might add, if he needs any help in expediting the evidence, I have numerous files on the subject.
I would like to explain to Hon. Members the amendment I proposed to this Bill, concerning clause 6(c) which stresses the development and application of forest management codes and standards, which were not adequate.

It was obviously not enough just to promote, we needed muscle in there. We needed government presence in there to monitor and ensure that the codes and standards were being followed. I hope that the government will go forth and carefully monitor, without impeding on the provincial governments' jurisidiction. It should be stressed that this monitoring be done in harmony with the provinces as well as the industry.
In the forestry sector the government seems to be very concerned about endangering its relations with the provinces. It is afraid to jade the provinces. I would like someone to indicate to me what is wrong with showing some direction. What is wrong with working with the provinces? By "working", I mean negotiate the strict

November 1, 1989
Government Orders
enforcement of quality reforestation, integrated forest management and do more research. Those provinces which do not comply will simply not have their forest resource development agreements renewed. In the same process, let them answer to their constituents. I am certain that both governments have the same common goal.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on the working paper prepared on September 8 this year by Dr. J.S. Maini, Assistant Deputy Minister (Policy), which deals with my amendment to clause 6 (c).
On page 7 of the working paper he mentions the following, under the heading: "The Challenge".
First, to make proper use of available knowledge to provide for integrated management of resources and create a national network of demonstration areas dedicated to integrated forest management.
Second, to intensify research on the potential impact on the forest environment of disruptions due to natural causes and human activity and to transmit the knowledge thus acquired.
Third, to enhance the productivity of woodlands in selected regions and increase the yield per hectare through improved management and enhanced protection of our forests, in such a way that multi-use of woodlands is possible.
Fourth, to reduce the waste produced by forest operations and wood processing. To rationalize the use of wood in various manufacturing processes leading to finished products.
Fifth, to undertake a systematic policy analysis, so as to better understand the decision-making process in the forestry sector and harmonize the various timeframes involved, bearing in mind economic, ecological, political and program considerations.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that the forestry sector is almost entirely a provincial responsibility. The provinces own about 80 per cent of our productive woodlands, the federal government only 12 per cent, while 8 per cent belongs to private landowners.
Although the vast majority of these lands belong to the provinces, this does not mean the federal government should renege on its responsibilities and leave everything up to the provinces.

My second proposed amendment was, as I expected, ruled out of order. I still wish to press the point that the forestry workers be protected. I am very concerned about the layoffs in the industry. Not enough is being done to retrain these people. I had proposed that training programs in co-operation with other departments be established for laid off workers.
We also need people in the forestry sector who have first-hand knowledge of the industry needs toward initiating training programs that would have a much higher rate of success than the current general programs offered. Taking into account the reason why my amendment was inappropriate, I caution the government that we on this side of the House will be vigilant in order to ensure that forestry workers be given the most chances to either recuperate their job or to have access to a training program geared to accommodate their talents and aptitudes.

I felt that adding "in co-operation with the other departments" to the amendment would have been enough. However, I hope the government will consider suggesting that the department in question propose a job recovery program specifically for workers who have been laid off in the forestry industry.

The third amendment that I proposed to this bill, I am pleased to say, received a favourable response from the government, so favourable I might add that the government proposed an identical one in substance. This clause deals in essence with exports and the competitiveness of Canadian forestry products on a global scale. It was mentioned briefly in clause 7(b) of the bill, but in a vague and unspecified manner. I had proposed to strengthen this.
When you take into account that the forest resource has an annual value of about $33 billion in goods shipped, the industry is also Canada's leading export sector, accounting for an annual net trade surplus in this sector of around $16 billion. As a result, the government
November 1, 1989

added section (e) to clause 6 stating "to seek to enhance the utilization of Canada's forest resources and the competitiveness of Canada's forest sector domestically and internationally."
I would like to say a few words on the interesting comments made by a witness who testified before the legislative committee on this bill. The witness, Mr. Leslie Reed, professor in industrial resources, faculty of forestry, University of British Columbia, stated five possible elements in a strategic plan. The first element was production targets that are doable and measurable. How much timber and non-timber do we want to have in the year 2000, 2020, 2050 and so on? It is pretty hard to talk about policy in a vacuum. We must think in terms of targets of predictable capacity.
On this I would like to point out that Canada's productive forests cover a total area of 220 million hectares or approximately 50 per cent of the area of this country. Over the years 12 per cent of those lands have not been satisfactorily restocked. We are looking at an increase of 240,000 hectares or nearly a 1 per cent per year increase in unforested land. Granted 88 per cent has been restocked. However this means that this year it may be 13 per cent, 14 per cent next year, and 15 per cent the next year.

We cannot let this kind of situation go on. Furthermore, according to the Auditor General's report for the fiscal year ending 31 March, 1988, at section 7.7:
Lack of adequate forest management in the past has resulted in depletion of the forest resource. Significant shortages of wood are now reported at the local level in every province. Restocking of productive forest lands has not kept pace with the harvest, and this threatens future forest productivity. Given the importance of the industry to Canada's economy and social structure, it is clear that any significant decrease in the supply of wood will have a serious impact on all Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, I may also add that since 1903, Sweden has had its "one for one" law which says that for every tree that is cut down, another one has to be planted. In Canada, similar legislation was passed for the first time in 1987, by the province of Quebec. In fact, there is a lot of catching up to do, and we must start today and take the lead.
The second point raised by Mr. Reed was priorities. There are a number of things we want to do. These
Government Orders
priorities should be ranked carefully. Our first priority should be silviculture and reforestation, as I said earlier.

His third point was an action plan that says in effect this is what we are going to do and these are the time frames we are working in. In 2 years, 5 years, 10 years, 25 years from now, this is where we expect to be. Too good to be true.
His fourth point was about accountability. We have to make someone accountable, someone to whom we can come back and make sure that the mandate indeed has been fulfilled.
I questioned Professor Reed on this point. I agreed with his term "accountability". I then asked how the federal government could be involved in such a process in perspective with the provincial jurisdiction in the Constitution. He replied that most reports talk about responsibility. This is a soft word. I prefer talking about accountability and enforcement, supervision, inspection and reporting. I think there is an easy way for the federal government to exercise leadership in a way that will soon have teeth. This goes back to my amendment "monitor and promote the development and application of forest management codes and standards".
His fifth and final point dealt with the monetary aspect. This is where the feedback, updating and change come in. Again this refers to my amendment which aims at supplying the necessary funds to guarantee the viability of our largest industry in Canada. This is where we will reap the benefits or, hopefully, not the disaster of our efforts.
I want to refer to comments by another witness who was invited to the legislative committee. Mr. Jim Cay-ford, executive director of the Canadian Institute of Forestry, gave a very good definition to the meaning of integrated management which was inserted as an amendment in clause 6, section (d).

By integrated management I mean, first of all, the management of Canada's forestry resources in terms of various products and services, and second, management in terms of lumber, fauna, environmental values, water, woodland areas and recreation. This is a very complex field, I have no doubt about that, and I would say that in

November 1, 1989
Government Orders
most cases, one use should take precedence over other uses in a particular area.
Increasingly, we will be faced with the following dilemma: Should governments promote the interests of industry or the environmentalists? Many misconceptions and misunderstandings are created by lack of direction and information. Elowever, I am convinced that in the long run, both parties will understand each other's values and will be able to reach a compromise.

Mr. Cayford went on to suggest several very good points. I will not state them all but I would very much like to quote the following:
We propose that the duties and functions of the minister should include specific reference to the establishment of an interdepartmental committee on forestry. This committee should be chaired by the Department of Forestry and have the responsibility to review all forestry programs of the federal government and to prepare an annual federal forestry budget.
I spoke to Mr. Cayford abut this suggestion. He indicated a requirement long overdue, that all the various national and provincial forest industry associations meet once or twice a year for information sessions. Government officials from the department and the minister's office would be present to listen to their concerns and proposed solutions to the different problems facing the forestry sector of our economy. Their contribution is extremely valuable because they deal with the forest on a daily basis.
What better way for the federal government to acquire all the current, up-to-date information and suggestions from the various sectors of the industry across the country. On this point, I have heard that the minister is very much in favour of such a conference. I would like to attend such a meeting, which I hope will take place in the very near future.
In conclusion, I would like to quote the words of Professor Reed:
Let us not kid ourselves. Either we have a commitment to forestry, either the provinces put up long-term strategic plans that have substance and then follow through in a courageous way, or they are not entitled to the federal sharing of funds.
This statement is in total agreement with what I have said earlier about the conditions that should be attached
to the federal contributions in the Forest Resource Development Agreements.
In closing, on September 26, at the second reading of this bill I said that under the Constitution Act, 1982, natural resources including forests are a provincial jurisdiction. From an environmental point of view, this does not mean the federal government should divest its responsibility for the forest sector. The industry needs us and national parks need the federal government. We should take our responsibilities and show strong leadership.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George-Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate today in third reading of Bill C-29, the long-awaited legislation to establish the department of forestry. As all members know, third reading is generally an opportunity to wrap up the discussion and debate and to review some of the amendments that have been made both in committee and in report stage to this most important legislation.
I say it is important because we heard a great deal in committee and in this House about just how much forestry impacts all of us, whether we live in northern British Columbia, northern Ontario, or in fact in downtown Toronto where a number of people depend on the forest for their cheques because of the wealth that our forests generate.
It would help us to remind ourselves of the over 300 communities that depend on the forest industry for their livelihood. It is the number one industry in this country, with some $38 billion generated annually. Some 840,000 Canadians are employed in all of the various forestry sectors. This bill and this debate is very important to many people in this country. It is a credit to this House that we have come to this point with this bill.
We have come to this point not without some work. The Prime Minister had promised this legislation some five years ago and we are finally just about there.
During discussion in committee, we pursued a number of the different clauses of the bill and questioned the minister who appeared on a number of occasions, and we thank him for that. We asked him if there was going to be more. This was housekeeping legislation, the government said, it was basically administrative in nature. Members on our side presented a number of amendments and, to use the words of one of the members, the
November 1, 1989

government liked the flavour of our amendments but chose at this time not to adopt those amendments or to support all of the amendments that we put forward.
You may not be aware, Mr. Speaker, that there have been discussions and the standing committee on forestry may be approaching yourself, Your Honour, and the important committees that decide these things to review the mandate of the department to talk to Canadians about forestry issues. Let us do that, and when we do and we hear from Canadians, let us be prepared. Let us get the commitment from the Prime Minister to enhance and strengthen the minister of forests' hand as is needed so that he can ensure that Canadians know that our forests, our national heritage if you like, are being well protected.
Just before I go into a couple of points specifically on the legislation, I want to read from a couple of letters from some of the people to whom I wrote and have been keeping up to date on the progress of this legislation. Let us hear what they had to say.
I am particularly pleased, for example, with a letter from the IWA of Canada which recently passed a new environmental policy. The IWA is aware of the importance of forests, not just for jobs but also with regard to the role that forests play in the environment and in our recreation. The letter is from Ms. Claire Dansereau, their environmental planner, commenting about our proposal for an annual forest ministers' conference and also for a conference every five years of the first ministers so that they can talk about our number one resource in this country.
They also supported our recommendation for a forest trade commissioner so that we would not get into the bind that this government has us in with the memorandum of understanding on the softwood lumber tariff. I will comment on that a little later.
All of the Canadians we know who live in our ridings and our communities talk to us about their jobs and the forests. They talk about the debate in the newspapers and on the radio and TV between environmentalists and the loggers, and ask how we are going to resolve this. They ask are we going to be able to use some of the responsible suggestions such as the one put forward by the leader of our provincial party, Mr. Harcourt, who has proposed a sustainable development policy so we can resolve those disputes.
Government Orders
I just want to read into the record a letter from Colin and Nelia Barnfield from Victoria. I extend my thanks to the member for Victoria who assisted here on Friday in the report stage of this bill. The letter states in part, "In order to be truly effective, we believe that a federal Department of Forestry should have the authority to stipulate precise management procedures for the sustainable development of the forests and lands over which it has jurisdiction and to be required to take appropriate legal action against any party which fails to follow these management procedures."
I know my friends in the Liberal party will support that because we have talked about it in committee. I know that when we get into the debate about our forest resource development agreements and how important they are to the replanting of our harvested lands, the intensive silviculture that has to take place, we will see that those standards are in place.
I am pleased that we did have an opportunity to present some amendments to this legislation that received the support of all parties and were passed. One that I am particularly proud of was the amendment I proposed that strengthens the minister's hand when it comes to the development of a public awareness program as it relates to our forests.
I think the polls are showing now that Canadians are aware more than ever of the importance of our environment. Of course, that goes hand in glove with the importance of our forests.
I suggest that we do not need a public awareness program that basically pats us on the back, that is just more rhetoric or pits the loggers against the environmentalists. I know the minister will certainly pay heed to a public awareness program-a national education program perhaps-that ensures all components of forests are considered when developing this awareness, most importantly for our young people.
I am also pleased with the amendment to clause 10 to the annual report provisions. When this legislation was first introduced in the House one of the first comments I made was that an annual report to Parliament should be an important event. It should not just go into the pile that ends up in the recycling bin. The filing of an annual report by the minister of forests should be an important event in this Chamber and give us the opportunity to debate some of the expanded areas that our amendment proposed. We talked about the need to have information, but it should not be restricted to information on

November 1, 1989
Government Orders
forest employment, which is often forgotten, as well as an inventory of Canada's forest lands.
In British Columbia we are talking about most of our province where we do not even know what is out there in our forested land. An inventory has not been done for 20 years. Our Ministry of Forests in British Columbia does not know what there is to cut out there. So that inventory is critical. It is important that we hear about that in this House.
A survey of the environmental standards should be applied by the forestry industry. All we have to do is to have watched the news last night and the headlines today. "Ottawa Condemns Alberta Pulp Mill Proposal". If this government and the provinces got their act together, then we might not run into this situation where we have projects proceeding. The federal official quoted in this article suggested that, "We"-meaning the federal government-"could not stop the project". This is a pulp mill proposal. We know the haste with which the provincial government in Alberta is proceeding on this matter. He stated that they could not stop the project from being built, but once built we could shut it down if it contravenes federal regulations.
If that is not an indication of the problem that we have with this government's inaction in putting together an environmental assessment procedure that is fair, that works with the provinces, industry and all concerned people, we are going to have ridiculous situations like this. We are going to continue to have these federal-provincial conflicts.
I should comment, while discussing the inventory of our old growth forests in our province and some of the new species that are becoming valuable as a resource now, that today there was a cabinet shuffle in our province and a new minister of forests was appointed. My colleagues from British Columbia would probably agree with me that anybody would be better than the last one. The last minister, frankly, was giving forestry a bad name. It is early, of course, to judge the new minister.
The message I have for the federal minister is that as quickly as possible he should meet with the new provincial forest minister to ensure that especially the discussions and the negotiations, whatever have been taking
place on the Forest Resource Development Agreement with B.C., get under way immediately.
One of the provisions in the legislation that gives the minister some authority to do some work-and this is a proposal I have that I think I would like the minister to consider-has to do with a lot of the resource use conflicts that we are hearing about. I think there is a certain degree of frustration, if you like, on the companies' part, on the part of people who work in the woods, the environmentalists, those concerned with native land claims, and, frankly, with the provincial governments. I am referring to the clause in the legislation where the minister is able to appoint committees.
It is my suggestion that he consider as one of the first actions to take a measure to appoint a committee upon the voluntary referral from any of the interested groups in these resource conflict areas that they sit and consider, collect and collate much of the federal information that is available from the federal government, its expertise in the forest research area and the economic development areas and, of course, the work that we hope is being done to settle land claims. I suggest we attempt to provide some outlet, if you like, for the frustration that I know is out there.
I think this would be a way for the federal minister to show his concern in this field and to give us an opportunity to work with those interested groups to ensure that these resource conflicts are resolved. We are respectful of provincial jurisdiction, but I think it is important, as the Minister of the Environment here has already offered to the province of B.C., to have assistance and research in the old growth when it relates to the Carmanah Valley. That is the kind of co-ordination I think we need.
I have not heard much yet about the department's work in single industry towns. My brief message there is to the minister and his department. Let us not just restrict it to sitting down and going through a few Statistics Canada reports and regurgitating information that has already been there. Let us get a chance to go and talk to some of these communities that are suffering now from a lack of wood supply. There are a number of mills in my home town that are suffering now. I would ask the minister and the government to consider much more seriously some of the work in the single industry
November 1, 1989

towns, a section of the Estimates that they have mentioned.
A lot of these communities are suffering. I was lucky to be in northern Ontario just a short time ago, in Thunder Bay and Kenora, where we talked about the forestry issues there and, in particular, the memorandum of understanding, the softwood lumber tariff and, of course, how this government sold out Canada's forests with that deal. As I said before, I hope Pat Carney is listening today because her government sold it out, with the help of the Prime Minister who said it was a good deal for Canada.
His own minister now recognizes, some couple of years later, that maybe we made a mistake. We are going to revisit the issue with the United States. I said: "It is about time". I said it in stronger words than that, but the editors at The Toronto Star edited out a few of the words. It is about time this government paid attention to the issue that the memorandum of understanding and that tariff is causing us.
In our province alone, the reporter mentions British Columbia accordingly jacked up its stumpage rates.
I managed to do a bit of research this morning with my colleague, the provincial member from Prince Rupert, Dan Miller, our provincial forest critic, to talk about what this has meant in B.C.
What has it meant in my part of the province? From the information I have prepared, basically because of the effect of the MOU by this government and by that crazy government in British Columbia, we have seen stumpage rate increases in northern Ontario of over 56 per cent. There is no flexibility built in. It is a hard and fast method. Obviously the social credit government and the Conservative government are in collusion on this. It is obviously one of the first issues that the federal minister should deal with, in consultation with the new minister. Let's get a move on. It has been too slow already.
The forest resource development agreements are dealt with in the legislation. We have spent a good amount of time in committee and in this House debating those agreements. The reason we are doing that is because they play such an important role for the federal government and the provincial governments to get together and help manage our resources.
Government Orders
This government has allowed these agreements to expire; six of them expired at the end of March. The minister is making his way along. We learn a little bit here and a little bit there about what the criteria is going to be. Who knows if this government really knows exactly what it is doing. The provinces, at least in western Canada, have identified some $400 million of their needs for forests. Yet we hear from this government that there might be $242 million available for all sectors, for all provinces.
I remind the minister that when he was on this side, as reported in the April 18, 1984 Hansard, of a question he put to the then Minister of the Environment. Of course the Liberals at the time were not sure just what to do with the minister of forests. At least the government across the way has agreed to create a full department of forests, not like the Liberals whose leader came to Prince George in the 1984 campaign and opposed a full department of forests.
The current minister, in a question to the then Minister of the Environment asked: "Is it really because the minister does not have the money to take to the bargaining table?" Well, I think the same comment could apply today. I think the minister responsible for western diversification who was here earlier will have to be held accountable sooner or later for the lack of help to our forests in western Canada.
In the few minutes I have left I want to wrap up about the importance of forestry to this country and to all members of Parliament, whether we are from urban or rural ridings. It is the minister of forests who should be the minister for sustainable development. Let us get his annual report on recycled paper. He should be the number one environmental department. As he says, the trees are the lungs of the earth. Well, our lungs work too.
The point I am making is that people have a livelihood from our forests and this minister should be responsible for that. He should be given the resources for that and the strength to do that.
In closing, I just want to say as a member of the committee I know that we are all sincere in our debate on this matter. I want to wish the staff of the new department well, because often they are the ones who do a lot of the work. I want to wish the minister well-not a lot-and we will see them all in committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise and comment on my colleague's address to this motion. I know that my colleague from Prince George-Bulkley Valley was responsible for the amendment to a motion increasing the public information component to this ministry.
As a member of the environment committee of this House I think it is crucial that there is more public information. We have heard very worrisome testimony in the environment committee about the kind of degradation of the forests and the relationship of that to the global warming, the phenomenon that is threatening us all.
I have a question for my colleague. The new minister of forests I trust will actually be the minister for sustainable development, particularly for the resource provinces like British Columbia from which we both come. How does he feel that that is actually going to be realized with this new ministry of forests?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend and colleague from Saanich-Gulf Islands who I know from our discussions has a great deal of concern over forests not only in the country and internationally but also in her own riding.
The first way to get that awareness out there, one simple way, is through the minister's annual report. It should be on recycled paper. It should be made available to schools across this country and to as many people as possible so that they can see what is taking place across the country.
He should sit down with his provincial forest ministers and provincial education ministers to see that the informational material on our forests is available to our schools. Even Adam Zimmerman thinks that we should get together and find that common data base so that we know what we are dealing with.
If we do not get that information to young people I think we may be doomed. I thank the member for her concerns in this regard. It is an excellent point. The way to hold the government accountable is in this Chamber and in the forestry committee where we will see that he gets the work done we want done.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add my words of praise to the work that the hon. member has done on this particular bill. I think he has done an excellent job of alerting the forestry community, certainly in western Canada and even in my province where I do not think he
has even visited the forests. However his name is certainly known there for the good work that he has done on this legislation.
I had the opportunity to work with the member on a proposal to the minister calling for the creation of community conservation brigades which would be groups of young people. We had proposed 12,000 from Canada who would be taken on as conservation brigades to fight fires, to plant trees and so on in the forested communities of the country.
I would just like the hon. member to comment on what prospects he might see for that kind of initiative being adopted.

Mr. Speaker, I too want to thank the member for Prince Albert-Churchill River. He is right, I have not visited his province yet. I hope to do that soon. I fly over it on the way home, so I have seen the big picture from time to time.
The member is right. He presented an excellent idea to the minister and to provincial ministers. We have received some favourable comment from some of the provincial ministers. I believe even the federal minister gave a little bit of a nudge and a wink in that direction.
As we work in developing these forest resource development agreements, I think that is a method and a way to deal with it. When the legislation is passed, it gives the minister the mandate to get on with the job. If he likes the idea, let us work together. I cannot think of a better way to do the public awareness that the member for Saanich-Gulf Islands talked about than through a conservation program that works with young people.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure and pride that I have participated in the debate on Bill C-29. I wish to take this opportunity to thank all individuals who participated in the process for their valuable contributions. I wish to congratulate the opposition for its fine performance.
I would especially like to highlight the important contribution of my colleague, the hon. member for Cochrane-Superior, his very valuable amendments, especially those dealing with the monitoring and promoting of the development and application of forest management codes and standards. I would also like to congratulate the member for Cochrane-Superior for his persistent fight against the 15 per cent export surtax on softwood lumber. My hon. colleague will certainly
November 1, 1989

agree that it is indeed a pleasure to have the opportunity of improving the government's legislation.
Last week, the Minister of State for Forestry expressed his appreciation for the amendment concerning the definition of sustainable development which I proposed during the committee deliberations. I would like to thank the minister for supporting my amendment. I am extremely pleased that he is finally beginning to see things my way.

Mr. Speaker, the definition of this expression in a bill, namely, that sustainable development means meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs, is a very significant step in dealing with the environment. Bill C-29 is the first piece of legislation in Canada to contain this definition.
As you no doubt know, Mr. Speaker, several groups have criticized the federal Government for using an expression that has no current definition and that can easily be misinterpreted. From now on, the Government will no longer be able to bandy this expression around thoughtlessly. Furthermore, my amendment will ensure that the Forestry Minister will play a key role in preserving Canada's precious woodlands.

The term sustainable development was originally coined in 1987 by the United Nations Royal Commission on Environment and Development chaired by the former Norwegian Prime Minister Dr. Gro Harlem Brund-tland. Indeed, the Brundtland report must take a great deal of the credit for the current and apparently high level of public concern about pollution and the global environment.
The report's main recommendation called for the international adoption of the concept of sustainable development, a blend of strong economic growth and environmental regulations aimed at preserving the planet as a hospitable habitat for mankind.
Government Orders
With respect to the forestry sector, the inclusion of a definition of sustainable development in this legislation will ensure that the forestry department will have regard to the conservation and effective management of our country's valuable forests. As the minister said in a CBC interview in Edmonton last week, and I quote: "Forests do more than sustain an industry; they sustain our environment". With that in mind and with a definition in law the foundation has been laid for the effective management and conservation of Canada's forests.
Although the forestry bill has been improved and strengthened by the diligent work of the opposition and the co-operation of the government members of the legislative committee, it still has several shortcomings. During committee deliberations many witnesses testified that the forestry sector was of such vital importance to Canada's economy that it needed a strong department to represent it.
The executive director of the Canadian Forestry Association, Mr. Glen Blouin, stated categorically that the mandate given to the forestry department ought to have been stronger and more all encompassing. "Such a mandate", he said, "would have reflected the significance of the forests to all Canadians in terms of the environment, balance of payments, employment, tourism and recreation".
Unfortunately what we have is a department with little clout. Mr. Blouin asked for the government to give the forestry department control of the vital forest resource development agreements, a mandate to provide leadership in all matters relating to forestry, along with a budget to reflect the importance of this new department. Instead, the department suffered a $28 million cut and a personnel reduction of 47 person-years in the budget tabled last spring.
Moreover, the minister still must run to other government agencies such as the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, western diversification and the Department of Industry, Science and Technology in order to obtain the money to fund forestry agreements with the provinces. Is that what you would call a strong department? Definitely not.
As I said earlier, the creation of a forestry department is of considerable importance in the recognition of the importance of this sector. Unfortunately this bill does

November 1, 1989
Government Orders
not provide the forestry sector the representation it needs. How could it, after all? The government is creating a department, yet it is reducing its resources.
In fact, forestry suffered an 11.9 per cent cut in the 1989-90 budget while all other natural resource based programs received budget increases. For example, the environment department's budget grew by 9.4 per cent. Energy, Mines and Resources received a 22.9 per cent increase. Fisheries and Oceans had its budget raised by 6 per cent, and agriculture received a 21.5 per cent increase.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker: Where is the government's commitment to forestry? It cannot go on setting up a department and then pull the rug out from underneath it. That just does not make sense.
If this new department is going to represent Canada's forestry sector effectively, it must receive a budget increase similar to those received by natural resource based programs.

Mr. Speaker, during the deliberations of the legislative committee on this Bill, the executive director of the Canadian Institute of Forestry, Mr. Jim Cayford, also said that the Government does not specify the new department's role clearly enough. He stated that the new department should have national responsibility, in that it should play a leading role in forestry, promote research and technology transfer, conclude federal-provincial agreements on forestry resource use, compile data on forest resources, conduct studies on the industry, marketing, trade and forestry economics, promote international forestry relations; set up programs concerning human resources management, employment and education; and, finally, make the public fully aware of this new project.
Talk about a tall order! However the new department will never be able to assume the leadership role described by Mr. Cayford unless its budget is geared to that kind of challenge.
The Minister told us that forests are among the priorities of his government, yet the only natural resources component has been downgraded. Why such disparity? Why would the government claim it will do more for the forest sector when in fact it will be doing less?
Our forests deserve better treatment. To a large extent, our country's growth can be traced back to this sector. It has been the foundation of our economy. Today still the forest industry remains one of the cornerstones of this nation. Nobody should underestimate the significance of the forest sector in our economy: Canada has 4.31 million square kilometres of forest, or about 176 square metres of forest for each of our 25 million inhabitants.
Close to 300,000 people earn their living directly in the forest sector, and it provides indirect work for about
750,000	other Canadians, including railway workers, truck drivers and heavy equipment operators in related fields.
Last year, productive forests made it possible for us to ship in excess of $30 billion worth of goods. One seventh of manufacturing revenues comes from a forest-related sector, and our forests account for more than $17 billion of Canada's net trade balance, more than agriculture, fisheries and mines put together.
Mr. Speaker, the great importance of the forestry industry for the Canadian economy requires much government leadership so that the Government can promote and enhance the health and viability of this sector. However, this Bill gives no weight or importance to the Department of Forestry, since it will have to obtain funds for forestry development agreements from other departments and agencies of the federal Government.
The federal-provincial forestry agreements with Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta expired on March 30. In addition, the agreements with Newfoundland, Quebec and British Columbia will lapse next March 30.
It is inconceivable for a government that says it supports the forestry sector to allow such a situation to occur. To date, these agreements have not been renegotiated. The Government must rectify this situation, because these agreements are vital for the future of Canada's forests.
Federal-provincial forestry agreements have provided over $1.1 billion for reforestation and management since 1985. More than 50 per cent of these funds come from the federal Government. These agreements will encourage increased forest management activities by providing

funds for ground preparation, tree-planting and plantation maintenance.

The Canadian Council of Forest Ministers issued a document in 1987 entitled "A National Forest Sector Strategy for Canada", calling on the federal government to improve and continue the forestry agreements. The federal government must take the upper hand in order to ensure that forest resource development becomes the cornerstone of Canada's forestry industry.
Although this bill as amended and reprinted, following the recommendations of the opposition, is much improved, it still provides the minister with responsibilities for the forestry agreements. Indeed, the minister's commitment to the agreements is somewhat shaky. When he appeared before the legislative committee, he expressed his reservations with respect to the forestry agreements. He said that whether or not the federal role in the forestry sector is best served by the agreements is an open question. He also said that the forestry agreements were, in his view, not the most effective way to manage the resource.
The Canadian Institute of Forestry has said that forest renewal must remain the essential element in future agreements, and that the agreements were very crucial to the future of the industry. Moreover, the Canadian Forestry Association has also said that the agreements are critical to the future of forestry in Canada.
How can a minister deny the importance of these agreements, while everybody agrees that they are extremely important? Does the minister know something we do not? If that is the case, I would appreciate him sharing that information with us.
The necessity of these agreements becomes even more clear when considering that world consumption of forest products is expected to increase substantially within the next 20 years. Without sound agreements to ensure the future of Canada's wood supply, there is no way that this country will be able to meet the demands of the future. Is that what the minister means by sustainable development?
It is very interesting to note that a study which was commissioned by the Canadian Forestry Service, the
Government Orders
Woodbridge-Reed report, neither addressed the environmental ramifications of forestry practices in Canada nor the urgent necessity of implementing adequate reforestation. All this study mentioned was that the forestry industry's output would increase over the next 20 years. Without adequate reforestation and without a continued commitment from this government to forestry agreements there will, quite simply, be no usable wood supply left in the next 20 years.
Why is the government establishing a forestry department? More importantly, is this government not taking the future of Canada's forestry sector seriously? Canada's forestry sector needs to be improved if it is to remain competitive with the rest of the world.
The 1988 Auditor General's report stated that three considerations directly affect decisions involving investment in reforestation. First, the vastness and great dispersal of the forest demand necessitates large expenditures for forest management. Second, federal investment in forestry usually also involves the provinces. Third, the growing cycle for mature forests involves a time span of between 40 to 80 years.
If the government claims that it wants to take the lead in the forestry sector, then its decision to manage and invest in forestry must reflect a commitment to a long-term view of the resource. The only way it can do this is to provide the minister with the responsibility for the forestry agreements. It must renew its commitments to these forestry agreements.
In conclusion, I would like to say that although we of the Liberal party support the principle of a full-fledged forestry department and agree that Bill C-29, as it now stands, is much improved because of the interventions of the opposition, we are duty bound to express many reservations which we have in regard to this legislation. The government is not out of the words with this one yet. It has voiced its commitment to the forestry sector. It has set up the department, although it has actually reduced its resources. It must now provide the strong leadership needed to ensure the health of this sector.
The opposition will be diligent and unrelenting in its endeavours to ensure that the government will give forestry the support which it needs and that it will live up to its commitments.

Mr. Speaker, I am extremely happy to have a chance to speak on this bill. I had hoped to be able to speak on second reading, but it ended fairly abruptly last week. It was with some pleasure that I realized I would have a chance to express a Saskatchewan perspective on the question of forestry.
It may come as a surprise to many members of this House and the people of Canada, if like my esteemed colleague from Prince George-Bulkley Valley, they have not visited the forests of Saskatchewan or flown over or driven through southern Saskatchewan, have the perception that there is not a tree in Saskatchewan. I know there are trees in Saskatchewan. I have planted about 2,000 of them on my farm. My family now has to look after those trees and they know that there are trees, at least on that patch of ground.
It is a little recognized fact, and one of the problems that the Saskatchewan forest industry faces, that 46 per cent of the land area of the province of Saskatchewan is in forests and 20 per cent of that is commercial forests. If you contrast that with 40 per cent in agriculture you realize that the commercial forests are half the size of the agricultural portion of Saskatchewan.
In my constituency of Prince Albert-Churchill River, 90 per cent is forested. It is a major issue in half of the geographic area of Saskatchewan. Through the years, it has been very difficult for that fact to be recognized, especially in our own province. Forestry is the second leading industry in Saskatchewan; 10 per cent of the gross provincial product comes from the forestry sector, both direct and indirect. In 1985, $290 million and probably more now, of income to the province was generated by the forests. As well, 8,000 people are employed in the forestry sector.
What happens in forestry is very important to the people of Saskatchewan, although it admittedly has not been a leading player in the forestry scene in Canada historically. Since agriculture is so dominant in Saskatchewan, that tends to be the leading economic debate. The population of the forested areas is sparse, therefore it does not have the numerical or political representation on the federal scene. It is a mere 6 per cent of the forests of Canada, and although it is a very significant land area and income generator that often does not get recognized.
It was, however, recognized by my predecessor, a former member for Prince Albert, the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker, who took a major initiative in this country by bring in the ARDA program in the late 1950s as an attempt to bring to life the economy of those communities that relied both on agriculture and forestry. That was a pioneering step, one which we should re-examine and perhaps consider reintroducing. In the context of the new department, some of those ideas might well be brought back.
I personally became involved with the forestry sector in Saskatchewan in 1982 when there was a major forestry congress in Saskatchewan. It was a very successful congress. The Saskatchewan Forestry Association, the industry and the unions, the IWA, the CPU, felt it was time that we as a sector in Saskatchewan took a hold of the situation, put our views on the record, analyzed what we had, and charted a common game plan.
At that time, the first round of FRDA agreements were in the process of negotiation and a large part of our intent was to create some kind of vehicle for input into that process. It turned out very well. The awareness within the province jumped to another level. Coupled with the activities that occurred as a result of that FRDA agreement, in many ways forestry has experienced its best seven years in the history in our province.
I would very much like to second the motion of my colleague for Prince George-Bulkley Valley that public information be a significant portion of the new department. It was an amendment that was adopted. I think activities like the forestry congress to launch the new FRDAs-and hopefully there are FRDAs-or to acquaint people with the activities of this department might well be a route to go. A congress like that every five years or so in every province is an excellent way to get the sector in thinking on the same wavelength.
FRDA had a funding level of $28 million, $14 million from the federal government, $14 million from the provincial government. It did some significant things. In firefighting, it allowed the development of a computer and a detection system that Saskatchewan did not have before. They purchased inventory and new equipment, trained people, and so on.
November 1, 1989

I have to confess that when the Auditor General said some provinces skimmed the FRDAs to carry on activities they should have been doing anyway, I thought that that applied in Saskatchewan, especially with reforestation. In 1982 the Devine government gutted the reforestation program. I know that because I live two miles from the forest nursery where they were burning trees and little seedlings because they did not have the money to plant them. Nevertheless, through this FRDA agreement, we are back up to the 10 million seedlings a year level. We need 20 to 25 million, however, to catch up on the backlog, because only half of our annual harvest is being reforested.
Also we started some initiatives in Indian forestry. A good portion of the land area in commercial forestry is either now on Indian reserves or potentially so if the claims are settled. As well, the Indian communities that are not reserve communities obtained some benefit from the fact that the Indian forestry was recognized as a sector with a training institute. Farm woodlots were also introduced, going back to the old ARDA idea.
The most critical aspect was the introduction of technical expertise to the province which we never had because we were a small industry. We did not have the personnel in many of the technical areas. FRDA brought together a critical mass of expertise that has been of tremendous benefit not only to the public sector of the communities, but to the private sector and the province as well.
We were disappointed when that did not come through. We were disappointed when we saw that there was only 28 per cent of the money available under the new regional development agreement in western Canada compared to what it was under the old ones, $242 million instead of $870 million. If that equation, 28 per cent, applies to the new FRDA in Saskatchewan, that would be a $4 million agreement, which would really be a pittance.
However, I have made representations to the minister of WDO. Somebody criticized the current structure, saying the ministry of forestry has to run all over to get its money. I think that is a valid critique, not to diminish the role of the minister of WDO, but it would be nice if forestry had its own money here. I have indicated to that minister that the two main priorities under the new
Government Orders
ERDA agreements, or children of ERDA, need to focus, first of all, on renewable resource sectors with forestry as the leading renewable resource sector. Second, we need the the development of organizational capacity at the community levels so that people can organize businesses and contracts to take advantage of opportunities and create opportunities for small businesses that utilize wood products. Third, we need to retain that expertise in the province that is so critical. We cannot do with any less. Even in that context we are happy that there is a department at least to relate to, and to start focusing some of that thinking.
Hopefully it will give some focus to the whole notion of sustainable development and the very critical role that the forest areas play in that. The vast majority of the land mass of the country is forested. How we treat that land mass is a very critical part of any attempt on our part to control climate change and to do our part to stop soil erosion. I think we have a real opportunity there.
Although we are supporting this legislation, perhaps we could offer some words of criticism with regard to the government's fundamental direction as is indicated here. The government ran on a platform, until it got sidetracked by free trade, of managing change. That is a very legitimate challenge for any government to take up. But I do not think, in all honesty, that this challenge is being met, certainly not in respect to the forest when only half of the reforestation is taking place that should be. Also, there is over-investment in capital in many cases for pulp mills. There has been huge private capital investment in plant and equipment that will not have the forest to process, or the wood product to process in a very few years. There has been a misdirection of resources. No matter what is the ideology of the government in something like forestry, it is its responsibility to make sure the investment is made in the right places. With all due respect, I do not think that this bill reflects the fact that the government realizes that.
There has not been nearly enough emphasis placed on benefiting the people who live in the forest, the communities of the forest. That is not only their physical environment, but their economic environment. I think that has often been lost.
In that context, I would like to mention that it has become widely noted that the hinterlands of Canada, the resource producing areas are being ignored. Even Ma-

November 1, 1989
Government Orders
clean's magazine saw fit to devote a cover story to the fact that the resource producing areas of this country, the hinterlands, and the people who do not live in big cities, are being ignored by this government. That is partly the result of 85 per cent of the land mass being represented by the opposition, and only 15 per cent by the government. It is starting to be reflected in the policies of the government.
For example, when one considers changes to the UI, increasing rates on fly-in food by 30 per cent, charging people $16,000 to $20,000 to get a private line phone, taking away the northern allowance, and what is happening to agriculture which often interrelates on the fringes of forestry, the communities of the forests are really hurting, in many cases, as a result of government policy. If there needs to be money invested, it would be best if it came from the people who actually lived there, but because of many of the government's actions they are not having the opportunity to do that.
In closing, I do appreciate the fact that we now have a department. I would again like to put on the record that the resources are woefully inadequate and that the forestry community, both the professional as well as the community at large are very disappointed. It has not been seen as a victory by people who are interested in the forests. It points out again that what this government has is not so much an image problem as a substance problem. This sums up as well as anything that all too many times we are getting an awful lot more image than we are substance. I challenge the government to take that into account as the process of evolving this department into full reality takes place.

speechtext: The hon. member for Prince George-Buckley Valley on a question or comment.

Mr. Speaker, I certainly appreciated the contribution the hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River made to the debate on this legislation. I know his concern for his riding and his province with regard to forestry. We have had many discussions on this topic. I take up his offer to visit Saskatchewan sometime rather than just flying over the province and get a chance to see some of those forests first hand and maybe even the nursery near where he lives. The hon. member is shaking his head in agreement, I am glad for that.
The member raised a question, and I am pleased to see that the minister responsible for western diversification is actually in the chamber right at the moment. The member mentioned that from what we have been able to glean so far, there appears to be a lack of funds available not only to forestry but other sectors in western Canada, as well as the funds that have to be shared with the provinces. The part of this that we often forget is the role that the provinces have in designing their priorities so that when they sit down with the federal minister, or federal counterpart, that they can work out some kind of priority listing. In B.C. we have already talked about our new forest minister and our hope that the federal minister and the new provincial minister will get together quickly.
I am interested in knowing if the Saskatchewan government puts a high priority on forestry. Do they see it as a sunset industry like some provinces do, as many Conservative provinces have, or are we looking at a government that is going to try and use this federal money to win a few more seats or buy off a few more people? Does the Devine government really care about forestry?

There is quite a difference between what one hears and what one sees. One hears a fair bit from the provincial government about its commitment to forestry, but really it has pretty much been restricted to helping companies like Weyerhaeuser which has turned out to be not a bad corporate citizen. Nevertheless, the energy has gone toward helping the corporate sector gain greater control of the forestry industry, with some modernization. They have really neglected reforestation, the community end, and the training end. In fact, what they have done has often been, quite frankly, at the expense of the forestry agreement. It was money they should have been spending anyway. In fact, covered under the agreement I think that it is a legitimate critique.
I might also reiterate that it is part of the problem of the Minister of Forestry having to go all over the place for money. For example, in the conservation brigades which we suggested, I thought it was a great idea to hire and train 1,000 young people in Saskatchewan in a constituency where $35 million a year is paid out in welfare. Approximately the same amount is paid out in unemployment insurance. We had fires burning out of control, and half the forests that should be replanted not being replanted. I thought devoting $6 million in Sas-

katchewan, a federal contribution, putting 1,000 young people to work accomplishing those tasks would surely be a good use of money. I think the government should have spent money on that, but as is so often the case everybody said it was a good idea but bureaucratically impossible.
We have to use this department. We have to give it enough authority to make sure that we can shake some of those bureaucratic trees so that what actually makes sense actually gets done.
